<pre-registration>
    <metadata>
        <title>Error Distribution Parameters in Visual Working Memory as Predictors of Visuospatial Cognitive Performance</title>
        <description>An online experiment examining whether individual differences in visual working memory error distributions, characterized by von Mises concentration parameters, predict performance on mental rotation tasks and self-reported visual imagery vividness. Participants complete a visual working memory task, mental rotation task, and visual imagery questionnaire to test whether distributional properties of recall errors capture meaningful cognitive differences beyond simple accuracy measures.</description>
        <contributors>Research team conducting visual working memory and spatial cognition research</contributors>

        <license type="select_one">
            <selected>CC-By Attribution 4.0 International</selected>
        </license>

        <subject>Cognitive Psychology, Visual Working Memory, Spatial Cognition, Individual Differences, Psychometrics</subject>
        <tags>visual working memory, mental rotation, spatial cognition, error distributions, von Mises, circular statistics, individual differences, visuospatial abilities</tags>
    </metadata>

    <study_information>
        <hypotheses>1. Individual differences in visual working memory error distributions, characterized by concentration parameters (κ) from von Mises fits, will predict mental rotation accuracy and reaction times (directional hypothesis: higher κ predicts better performance). This hypothesis is theoretically grounded in resource-based models of visual working memory (Bays & Husain, 2009; Ma et al., 2014) which propose that precision reflects allocation of a limited cognitive resource. If spatial abilities share common precision-based mechanisms, individuals with higher VWM concentration parameters should demonstrate superior spatial transformation abilities. 2. Participants with higher concentration parameters will demonstrate superior mental rotation performance, particularly for larger angular disparities where precise spatial transformations are most demanding (directional hypothesis: interaction between κ and rotation angle). This prediction follows from the theoretical framework that spatial transformations requiring greater precision should be more sensitive to individual differences in precision mechanisms, creating stronger relationships at larger rotation angles. 3. Higher concentration parameters will correlate positively with VVIQ2 imagery vividness ratings (directional hypothesis: positive correlation). This hypothesis is based on theories linking spatial precision to imagery abilities (Kosslyn et al., 2006) and evidence that objective precision measures correlate with subjective imagery ratings (Zeman et al., 2020). 4. These relationships will persist after controlling for domain-general factors including overall accuracy, response consistency, and engagement metrics (directional hypothesis: κ maintains predictive power after controls). This hypothesis tests whether precision-specific mechanisms account for unique variance beyond general cognitive factors that could drive task correlations.</hypotheses>
    </study_information>

    <design_plan>
        <study_type type="select_one">
            <selected>Experiment</selected>
        </study_type>

        <blinding type="select_multiple">
            <selected>
                - Personnel who analyze the data collected from the study are not aware of the treatment applied to any given group.
            </selected>
        </blinding>
        
        <additional_blinding>No additional blinding beyond analyst blinding is implemented in this study.</additional_blinding>
        <study_design>This is a within-subjects correlational design examining individual differences across three tasks: Visual Working Memory (VWM), Mental Rotation Task (MRT), and Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire 2 (VVIQ2). The VWM and MRT tasks are counterbalanced across participants using JavaScript randomization. The design involves repeated measures within the MRT (multiple rotation angles per participant) and extraction of individual-level parameters from VWM error distributions. No experimental manipulation is applied; instead, naturally occurring individual differences in VWM precision parameters serve as the primary predictor variable.</study_design>
        <randomization>Task order (VWM vs MRT) will be randomized using JavaScript randomization implemented in Pavlovia.org with the specific code 'if (Math.random() < 0.5)...', with participants randomly assigned to complete either VWM-first or MRT-first sequences. The VVIQ2 questionnaire will always be completed last via SurveyMonkey link.</randomization>
    </design_plan>

    <sampling_plan>
        <existing_data type="select_one">
            <selected>Registration prior to creation of data</selected>
        </existing_data>
        
        <data_collection_procedures>Participants will be recruited via Prolific with inclusion criteria: adults aged 18-35, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, native English speakers, Prolific approval rating ≥95%. Exclusion criteria: self-reported neurological conditions. Compensation will be set at £9 per hour (pro-rata for estimated 40-minute session). The experiment will be implemented on Pavlovia.org with browser window dimension checks (minimum 768x768 pixels), fullscreen mode monitoring (flagged but not enforced), and comprehensive data collection including trial-level responses, browser metadata (type, OS, frame rate), and engagement metrics consisting of exactly four aggregate measures: total instances and duration of focus loss during instructions, and total instances and duration of focus loss during trials.</data_collection_procedures>
        <sample_size>Target sample size is 130 participants, accounting for anticipated exclusions and attrition in the online environment.</sample_size>
        <sample_size_rationale>Power analysis using the pwr package in R targeted detection of medium effect size (Cohen's f² = 0.15) for both mixed-effects models (MRT analysis) and multiple regression models (VVIQ2 analysis) with power = 0.80 and α = 0.05. Initial calculated sample size was 91 participants. Final sample size of 130 includes 30% inflation to account for anticipated participant exclusions and attrition in online data collection.</sample_size_rationale>
        <stopping_rule>Data collection will continue until 130 participants complete the full protocol or until recruitment resources are exhausted, whichever occurs first. Real-time monitoring of data quality will be conducted throughout recruitment.</stopping_rule>
    </sampling_plan>

    <variables>
        <manipulated_variables>No variables are experimentally manipulated in this correlational study. Individual differences in visual working memory precision serve as naturally occurring predictor variables.</manipulated_variables>
        <measured_variables>Primary predictor: VWM concentration parameter (κ) from von Mises distribution fits to orientation recall errors. Primary outcomes: MRT accuracy (proportion correct) calculated as number of correct responses divided by total valid trials per rotation angle (0°, 50°, 100°, 150°), MRT reaction times (milliseconds from stimulus onset to keypress) for correct responses only, VVIQ2 total score (sum of all 32 items, range 32-160) and subscale scores (sum of 4 items per scenario, range 4-20 each). Control variables: mean VWM accuracy (proportion of trials with absolute error ≤15°), response time coefficient of variation (standard deviation of response times divided by mean response time within participants), composite engagement score derived from standardized focus loss and timeout metrics. Additional measures: VWM bias parameter (μ) from von Mises fits, browser metadata (type, OS, frame rate), session duration, demographic information from Prolific.</measured_variables>
        <indices>VWM concentration parameter (κ) extracted via maximum likelihood estimation of von Mises distributions fitted to individual participants' orientation recall errors after mixture modeling to separate precision-limited from non-precision responses using a modified approach that tests cardinal bias rather than uniform guessing. Composite engagement score calculated by standardizing timeout rate (proportion of timeout trials across both tasks) and total focus loss duration during trials, then averaging these standardized components. Response time coefficient of variation measured as within-participant standard deviation divided by within-participant mean for valid trials only.</indices>
    </variables>

    <analysis_plan>
        <statistical_models>1. VWM error modeling: Modified two-component mixture models using mixtools R package to separate precision-limited responses from responses showing cardinal bias (concentrations around 0°, 45°, 90°, 135°) rather than uniform guessing. Model comparison using AIC/BIC will test uniform vs. cardinal-biased vs. wrapped normal guess components. Von Mises distribution fitting using circular package with maximum likelihood estimation to extract κ and μ parameters per participant, with convergence diagnostics including gradient tolerance <1e-6, maximum 1000 iterations, and multiple starting values. 2. MRT analysis: Linear mixed-effects models using lme4 package with MRT accuracy (logistic link function) and log-transformed reaction time as dependent variables, κ as primary predictor, rotation angle as categorical predictor, κ×rotation angle interaction, random intercepts for participants, and control variables as covariates. Model diagnostics will include residual plots, normality tests, and leverage assessments. 3. VVIQ2 analysis: Hierarchical multiple regression with VVIQ2 total score as dependent variable, control variables in first block, κ in second block, using robust regression (Huber's M-estimation with tuning constant k=1.345). 4. Sensitivity analyses: Alternative circular distributions (wrapped normal, wrapped Cauchy) tested using 10-fold cross-validation; analyses repeated after excluding responses identified as cardinal-biased; bootstrap resampling (n=1000) to propagate uncertainty from mixture modeling and von Mises fitting stages.</statistical_models>
        <transformations>Orientation errors normalized to ±90° range using the formula: normalized_error = ((response_angle - target_angle + 90) mod 180) - 90. MRT reaction times log-transformed using natural logarithm after removing values <200ms. Control variables (accuracy, response time variability, timeout rate, focus loss duration) z-score standardized within sample before analysis. VVIQ2 items requiring reverse-coding will be transformed using: reversed_score = 6 - original_score.</transformations>
        <inference_criteria>Two-tailed tests with α = 0.05 for all primary analyses. Family-wise error rate control using Holm-Bonferroni correction applied across the full set of 13 primary comparisons: 4 MRT accuracy tests (one per rotation angle), 4 MRT reaction time tests, 1 VVIQ2 total score test, and 4 sensitivity analyses with alternative circular distributions. Effect sizes reported with 95% confidence intervals: Cohen's f² for regressions, partial η² for mixed models, Cohen's d for paired comparisons. Marginal and conditional R² values calculated for mixed-effects models using r.squaredGLMM function.</inference_criteria>
        <data_exclusion>Session-level exclusions: total session duration >3 SD from sample mean, total focus loss instances during trials >95th percentile of sample distribution (replacing arbitrary 10-instance threshold). VWM exclusions: <50% valid trials (reduced from 70% to prevent range restriction) after removing practice/timeout/RT<200ms trials, mean absolute error >3 SD above sample mean, mixture model convergence failure or von Mises fitting failure. MRT exclusions: overall accuracy <25% (reduced from 50% to prevent range restriction), trial-level RT outliers >3 SD from participant's mean per rotation angle, mean RT >3 SD from sample mean (increased from 2.5 SD to reduce exclusions). VVIQ2 exclusions: incomplete questionnaires, invariant response patterns (all items rated identically), completion time <90 seconds (increased from 2 minutes based on 4 items per minute reading rate).</data_exclusion>
        <missing_data>No missing data expected for primary measures as all survey questions are required. Participants with incomplete task data will be excluded according to the data exclusion criteria specified above. Any participants excluded due to technical failures will be replaced through continued recruitment.</missing_data>
        <exploratory_analysis>Investigation of whether specific rotation angles show stronger relationships with κ parameters beyond the planned interaction analysis. Examination of relationships between browser frame rate and task performance measures. Content analysis of any systematic patterns in mixture model failures or von Mises convergence issues. Assessment of whether exclusion patterns differ systematically between task orders or demographic groups.</exploratory_analysis>
    </analysis_plan>

    <other>This research bridges cognitive psychology, psychometrics, and computational modeling by connecting behavioral error distributions to individual differences in spatial abilities. Model convergence diagnostics specified: gradient tolerance <1e-6, log-likelihood change <1e-8 between iterations, successful convergence across 5 different random starting values for mixture models. Software specifications: R version 4.3.0 or higher, mixtools package version 1.2.0, circular package version 0.4-95, lme4 version 1.1-30. Computational reproducibility ensured through set.seed(12345) for all random processes, detailed session info recording, and archived analysis code with package version documentation. Bootstrap procedures for uncertainty propagation will use 1000 resamples with bias-corrected and accelerated confidence intervals. Alternative circular distribution testing will include wrapped normal, wrapped Cauchy, and von Mises distributions, with model selection based on cross-validated log-likelihood.</other>
</pre-registration>
